results.question: Do creatures phasing back in trigger enter the battlefield abilities?
results.text: No, creatures phasing back in do not trigger enters-the-battlefield abilities. results.question: how does trample work with deathtouch?
results.text: When a creature with trample and deathtouch deals combat damage, deathtouch modifies how lethal damage is determined. Any amount of damage dealt by a source with deathtouch is considered lethal damage for the purposes of determining excess damage [702.2c]. Trample allows the controller of an attacking creature to assign combat damage first to blocking creatures. Once all blocking creatures have been assigned lethal damage, any excess damage can be assigned to the player, planeswalker, or battle the creature is attacking [702.19b]. Because deathtouch makes any amount of damage lethal, even 1 damage from a creature with deathtouch and trample would be considered lethal to a blocker. This means that any remaining damage from that creature can be assigned as excess damage to the defending player, planeswalker, or battle [702.2c, 702.19b, 120.4a].

results.question: is storm a triggered ability that can be countered?

results.question: can i use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a commander deck that only has one of those colors?

If your commander's color identity is only red, you could include a card with {R/G} in your deck because red is one of the colors in the {R/G} hybrid symbol, and red is present in your commander's color identity [903.5c].

results.question: can I respond to the untap step?
results.text: No, you cannot respond to the untap step. No player receives priority during the untap step, which means no spells can be cast and no abilities can be activated or resolve. Any abilities that trigger during the untap step are held until the next time a player would receive priority, typically during the upkeep step. The untap step ends when all its specified actions are completed, as no players receive priority during this step.

results.question: are creatures still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step?
results.text: Yes, creatures are still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step. A creature remains an attacking creature until it is removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first. The end of combat step is part of the combat phase, and creatures are only removed from combat at the end of that step if they leave the battlefield, their controller changes, they phase out, an effect specifically removes them, or they are a planeswalker or battle being attacked and stop being so, or if they are an attacking or blocking creature that regenerates, stops being a creature, or becomes a battle. [508.1k], [508.4], [508.4b], [508.4d], [506.4a], [Attacking Creature]

results.question: Do you cast lands?

results.question: can I sacrifice an evoked creature before that creature's evoke triggered ability resolves?
results.text: No, you cannot sacrifice an evoked creature before its evoke triggered ability resolves. The evoke ability is a triggered ability that goes on the stack when the permanent enters the battlefield [702.74a]. You can only sacrifice a creature as a cost for an ability or spell if that cost is being paid at that time [702.48b]. Since the sacrifice is part of the resolution of the evoke triggered ability, you cannot sacrifice the creature before that ability resolves.

results.question: if a card loses all abilities, does that include keyword abilities?
results.text: Yes, if a card loses all abilities, this includes keyword abilities. Keyword abilities are a type of ability, and effects that remove abilities remove all instances of them [113.10b]. For example, if a permanent loses banding, it also loses all "bands with other" abilities [702.22b]. Similarly, losing hexproof causes an object to lose all "hexproof from [quality]" abilities [702.11e].

results.question: can i draw cards if i'm already at my maximum hand size?
results.text: You can draw cards even if you are at your maximum hand size. However, during your cleanup step, you must discard cards until your hand size is equal to your maximum hand size. If an effect instructs you to draw cards and your library is empty, you will draw the remaining cards and then lose the game the next time a player would receive priority. If an effect attempts to move cards from your library to your hand without using the word "draw," and your library is empty, it will move as many cards as possible. If an effect replaces a card draw, it applies even if no cards can be drawn because your library is empty.

results.question: what happens when a planeswalker has 0 or less loyalty counters?
results.text: When a planeswalker has 0 loyalty counters, it is put into its owner's graveyard. This is a state-based action. Damage dealt to a planeswalker causes that many loyalty counters to be removed from it.

results.question: do non-creature artifacts die?
results.text: The term "dies" specifically applies to creatures and planeswalkers. It means that a creature or planeswalker is put into a graveyard from the battlefield [Dies, 700.4]. Non-creature permanents, such as artifacts, do not die. If an artifact is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, it has not died unless an effect specifically states that it dies.

results.question: what happens if i should draw a card when my library is empty?
results.text: If you are required to draw a card and your library has no cards left, you draw the remaining cards (which is zero cards in this case) and then lose the game the next time a player would receive priority. This is a state-based action. If an effect offers you the choice to draw a card when your library is empty, you can choose to do so. However, if another effect prevents you from drawing cards, you cannot choose to draw a card. If an effect moves cards from your library to your hand without using the word "draw," you have not drawn those cards, and this does not cause you to lose the game if your library is empty.

results.question: what are the steps in combat and when do I have priority as the defending player?
results.text:
The combat phase consists of five steps: beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, combat damage, and end of combat [506.1]. The declare attackers and combat damage steps are skipped if no creatures are declared as attackers or put onto the battlefield attacking [506.1]. There are two combat damage steps if any attacking or blocking creature has first strike or double strike [506.1].

In a two-player game, the nonactive player is the defending player [506.2]. In a multiplayer game, if not all opponents automatically become defending players, the active player chooses one opponent to be the defending player during the beginning of combat step [703.4h, 507.1]. If the "Attack Multiple Players Option" is in play, all opponents are defending players [802.2].

You, as the defending player, receive priority during the beginning of combat step after any turn-based actions have been dealt with and abilities that trigger at the beginning of that step have been put on the stack [117.3a]. You also receive priority during the end of combat step [511.1].

results.question: can i respond to a mana ability?
results.text: No, you cannot respond to a mana ability. Mana abilities do not use the stack, which means they cannot be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to. They resolve immediately after they are activated or triggered. [605.3b], [605.4a], [405.6c]

results.question: can I respond to a cost being paid?
results.text: You cannot respond to a cost being paid. The rules state that paying costs is part of the process of casting a spell [601.2g], declaring attackers [508.1j], declaring blockers [509.1f], or activating an ability [602.4]. Once a player has begun to pay costs, they must complete the payment, and partial payments are not allowed [509.1f, 508.1j, 601.2h]. results.question: can you explain layers?
results.text:
Layers are a system used to determine the order in which continuous effects are applied to objects in Magic: The Gathering [Layer]. Continuous effects are applied in a series of layers, and within each layer, effects are applied in sublayers, then by timestamp order, unless a dependency alters this order [613.1, 613.2c, 613.8]. The layers are as follows:

Layer 1: Rules and effects that modify copiable values are applied. This includes copy effects and effects that merge an object with a permanent. After this layer, an object's characteristics are its copiable values [613.1a, 613.2c].
Layer 2: Control-changing effects are applied [613.3].
Layer 3: Text-changing effects are applied [613.1c].
Layer 4: Type-changing effects are applied, including changes to card types, subtypes, and supertypes [613.1d].
Layer 5: Color-changing effects are applied [613.1e].
Layer 6: Ability-adding effects, keyword counters, ability-removing effects, and effects that prevent abilities are applied [613.1f].
Layer 7: Power and toughness modifying effects are applied. This layer has several sublayers:
Layer 7a: Effects from characteristic-defining abilities that define power and/or toughness are applied [613.4a].
Other sublayers within Layer 7 apply effects in timestamp order [613.4a]. For example, a +1/+1 counter is applied in layer 7c, followed by a spell that grants +4/+4, then an enchantment that grants +0/+2, and finally an effect that sets power and toughness to 0/1, with the final result determined by the order of application [613.5].

Some effects span multiple layers. For instance, an effect that grants +1/+1 and changes color applies the color change in layer 5 and the power/toughness bonus in layer 7c [613.6]. Similarly, an effect that changes an artifact to a creature and sets its power/toughness applies the type change in layer 4 and the power/toughness change in layer 7b [613.6].

results.question: how does the legend rule work?
results.text: The legend rule is a state-based action that applies when a player controls two or more legendary permanents that share the same name. In this situation, the player must choose one of those permanents to keep, and all the others are put into their owners' graveyards. This rule applies to any permanent with the supertype "legendary," including planeswalkers that have received errata to have this supertype [Legend Rule, 704.5j, 205.4d, 306.4].

results.question: when does my creature die after its been marked with a lethal amount of damage?
results.text: A creature with lethal damage marked on it is destroyed as a state-based action [120.6, 302.7, 704.5g]. State-based actions are checked automatically whenever a player would receive priority, or during the cleanup step [704.3, 514.3a]. If a creature has lethal damage marked on it, it will be destroyed at that time [704.5g]. Damage marked on a creature is removed during the cleanup step [120.6, 514.2].

results.question: can I cast my commander from exile?
results.text: Yes, you can cast your commander from exile in a Commander game. If your commander is in the graveyard or in exile, and it was put into that zone since the last time state-based actions were checked, you may put it into the command zone. This is a state-based action. Additionally, some effects allow you to cast spells from exile, and if your commander meets the criteria of such an effect, you may cast it. Cards exiled face down can be cast if you are allowed to look at them and the spell has the specified qualities.

results.question: what happens during the cleanup step?
results.text: During the cleanup step, all damage marked on permanents is removed, and all "until end of turn" and "this turn" effects end. These actions happen simultaneously and do not use the stack [514.2]. Normally, no player receives priority during the cleanup step, meaning no spells can be cast and no abilities can be activated [514.3]. However, if state-based actions need to be performed or triggered abilities are waiting to be put on the stack, those actions are performed, the abilities are put on the stack, and then the active player receives priority. If this happens, players may cast spells and activate abilities. Once the stack is empty and all players pass in succession, another cleanup step begins [514.3a]. If no state-based actions are performed and no triggered abilities are waiting to be put on the stack during the cleanup step's initial check, the step ends without any player receiving priority [704.3].

results.question: when are state-based actions checked?
results.text: State-based actions are checked throughout the game and happen automatically whenever certain conditions are met [704.2, 704.1a, State-Based Actions]. They are dealt with before a player would receive priority [117.2d, 405.6f]. Specifically, each time a player would get priority, the game first performs all applicable state-based actions as a single event [117.5]. This process repeats until no more state-based actions are performed [117.5]. State-based actions are also checked during the cleanup step [704.3]. Additionally, they are checked when an effect ends the combat phase or ends the turn [724.2c, 724.1c]. Turn-based actions, which happen before state-based actions are checked, occur at the beginning of each step and phase, and also when each step and phase ends [703.3, 405.6e].

results.question: when can I concede a game?
results.text: A player may concede the game at any time. Conceding causes that player to leave the game immediately and lose the game. This is true even if another player controls you, or if you are playing in a Two-Headed Giant game where your team will leave the game and lose. The only exception to this rule is that a card's text that directly contradicts the rules takes precedence, unless that card's text is about conceding, in which case a player can still concede at any time.

results.question: how do I know who the active player is?
results.text: The active player is the player whose turn it is [Active Player]. In a multiplayer game using the shared team turns option, the active team is the team whose turn it is, and each other team is a nonactive team [Active Team]. If multiple players would make choices or take actions at the same time, the active player makes their choices first, followed by the other players in turn order [101.4e]. Any ability that refers to the "active player" refers to one specific active player, and the ability's controller chooses which one at the time its effect is applied [805.9].

results.question: when someone other than the active player casts a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text: When a player who is not the active player casts a spell, the active player receives priority first. This is because the active player generally receives priority after a spell resolves [117.3b]. If multiple players would make choices or take actions at the same time, the active player makes their choices first, followed by other players in turn order [101.4d, 101.4e].

results.question: when the active player cast a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text: When the active player casts a spell, that player receives priority afterward. This is because casting a spell is an action for which the active player would normally receive priority, and rule [117.3c] states that if a player has priority when they cast a spell, that player receives priority afterward.

results.question: can I hold priority to cast more spells after I've cast one or more spells?
results.text: You can hold priority to cast more spells after you've cast one or more spells if the spell you are resolving instructs or allows you to cast another spell during its resolution. In this specific case, no player receives priority after the new spell is cast, and the current spell or ability continues to resolve. However, under normal circumstances, after a spell resolves, the active player receives priority [117.3b]. If you cast a spell, you receive priority afterward [117.3c]. When casting a spell, after the steps for casting are completed and effects that modify the spell are applied, the spell becomes cast. If you had priority before casting it, you get priority again [601.2i].

results.question: when are lore counters put on sagas?
results.text: Lore counters are put on Sagas in two ways. First, when a Saga enters the battlefield, it gets lore counters based on whether it has "read ahead." If it has read ahead, its controller chooses a number between one and its final chapter number, and the Saga enters with that many lore counters [714.3b]. If it does not have read ahead, it enters with one lore counter [714.3a]. Second, as a player's precombat main phase begins, that player puts a lore counter on each Saga they control that has one or more chapter abilities [714.3c, 505.4, 703.4f]. This is a turn-based action and does not use the stack [703.4f, 505.4].

results.question: what is a delayed triggered ability?
results.text: A delayed triggered ability is an ability created by effects that will do something later in the game, rather than when the spell or ability that created it resolves [Delayed Triggered Ability]. These abilities are created during the resolution of spells or abilities, as the result of a replacement effect being applied, or as the result of a static ability that allows a player to take an action [603.7a]. A delayed triggered ability will contain "when," "whenever," or "at," though that word won't usually begin the ability [603.7]. It will trigger only once, the next time its trigger event occurs, unless it has a stated duration [603.7b]. If a spell creates a delayed triggered ability, that spell is its source, and the player who controlled the spell as it resolved is its controller [603.7d]. If an activated or triggered ability creates a delayed triggered ability, the source and controller are the same as the original ability [603.7e]. If a static ability generates a replacement effect that creates a delayed triggered ability, the object with the static ability is the source, and the controller of that object when the replacement effect was applied is the controller of the delayed triggered ability [603.7f]. If a static ability allows a player to take an action and creates a delayed triggered ability if they do, the object with the static ability is the source, and the controller of that object when the action was taken is the controller of the delayed triggered ability [603.7g]. A delayed triggered ability that refers to a particular object still affects it even if the object changes characteristics, but it won't affect the object if it's no longer in the zone it's expected to be in when the delayed triggered ability resolves [603.7c]. If a delayed triggered ability refers to X, and X was chosen for the cost of the spell or ability that created it, the value of X for the triggered ability is the same as the value chosen for the spell or ability [107.3n]. A resolving spell or ability may also create reflexive triggered abilities that follow the rules for delayed triggered abilities, but they are checked immediately after being created [603.12]. A delayed triggered ability is controlled by the player who controlled its source at the time it triggered [603.3a].

results.question: can non-permanent spells have abilities?
results.text: Yes, non-permanent spells can have abilities. Abilities of an instant or sorcery spell usually function while that object is on the stack [113.6]. Some static abilities can apply while a spell is on the stack, such as those that modify how the spell can be played or cast [604.5, 113.6e]. Additionally, effects can cause spells to gain abilities as they are cast [610.5]. When a spell is cast, it is put on the stack [601.2a]. Activated and triggered abilities that are on the stack are objects and can be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities [113.1c, 113.9].

results.question: can I use a mana ability when a spell with split-second is on the stack?
results.text: Yes, you can use a mana ability when a spell with split second is on the stack. Split second is a static ability that prevents players from casting other spells or activating abilities that aren't mana abilities while the spell with split second is on the stack [702.61a]. Mana abilities do not use the stack and resolve immediately [113.4, 405.6c]. Players may activate mana abilities whenever they have priority, or when casting a spell or activating an ability that requires a mana payment, or when a rule or effect asks for a mana payment, even in the middle of casting or resolving a spell or activating or resolving an ability [605.3a, 117.1d].

results.question: [Counterspell] is on top of the stack targeting my [Divination]. When everyone passes priority, what resolves first, and does Divination still resolve?
results.text: When everyone passes priority, the spell or ability on top of the stack resolves [608.1]. In this scenario, Counterspell is on top of the stack, and it is an instant spell [112.1]. Counterspell targets Divination, which is also a spell on the stack [112.1]. When Counterspell resolves, it will counter Divination [701.6a]. To counter a spell means to cancel it, removing it from the stack so it does not resolve and none of its effects occur [701.6a]. Therefore, Divination will not resolve.

results.question: My [Charging Rhino] has trample and is blocked by [Vampire Nighthawk], which has deathtouch. How much combat damage do I have to assign to the blocker before I can trample the rest over to the player?
results.text: When your Charging Rhino, which has trample, is blocked by a Vampire Nighthawk with deathtouch, you must assign lethal damage to the Vampire Nighthawk before assigning any excess damage to the player. Lethal damage is an amount of damage greater than or equal to a creature's toughness [Lethal Damage]. Since the Vampire Nighthawk has deathtouch, any amount of damage you assign to it is considered lethal damage [702.2c]. Therefore, you must assign at least 1 damage to the Vampire Nighthawk to satisfy the lethal damage requirement. Any damage beyond that 1 point can be assigned to the defending player [702.19b].

results.question: I have [Monastery Swiftspear] on the battlefield and I cast [Shardless Agent]. When its cascade ability puts a noncreature spell onto the stack, does Monastery Swiftspear's prowess trigger before or after that cascaded spell resolves?
results.text: When Shardless Agent is cast, its cascade ability triggers and resolves before Shardless Agent itself does [Shardless Agent ruling #1]. If the cascade ability results in a noncreature spell being cast, that spell is put onto the stack. Prowess triggers when you cast a noncreature spell [702.108a]. Therefore, the prowess ability triggers when the cascaded spell is cast. Prowess triggers go on the stack on top of the spell that caused them to trigger and resolve before that spell [Monastery Swiftspear ruling #2]. Thus, Monastery Swiftspear's prowess will trigger and resolve before the cascaded spell resolves.

results.question: My opponent's [Grizzly Bears] has 2 damage marked on it. Do state-based actions make it die before my [Lightning Bolt] resolves?
results.text: State-based actions are checked automatically whenever a player would receive priority, and they happen before a player receives priority [117.2d, 405.6f, 704.3]. Damage marked on a creature is checked to see if it's lethal during the state-based action check [704.5g]. If a creature has damage marked on it equal to or greater than its toughness, it is destroyed as a state-based action [120.6, 302.7, 704.5g]. Damage itself does not destroy a creature; rather, state-based actions do so as a result of the damage [120.5]. Since your Lightning Bolt has not yet resolved, it has not dealt damage, and therefore state-based actions would not yet destroy the Grizzly Bears based on the 2 damage already marked on it. State-based actions are checked after your Lightning Bolt resolves and deals its damage.

results.question: It's my upkeep. My [Phyrexian Arena]'s beginning-of-upkeep trigger and my opponent's own beginning-of-upkeep trigger both want to go on the stack. Who chooses the order, and when exactly do they trigger?
results.text: Both your Phyrexian Arena's trigger and your opponent's beginning-of-upkeep trigger trigger at the beginning of your upkeep step [500.6]. They are put onto the stack the next time a player would receive priority [500.6]. Since you are the active player, you receive priority first at the beginning of your upkeep [503.1a]. When multiple triggered abilities have triggered since the last time a player received priority, each player, in APNAP order (Active Player, Non-Active Player), puts each triggered ability they control onto the stack in any order they choose [603.3b]. Therefore, you would put your Phyrexian Arena's trigger on the stack first, and then your opponent would put their trigger on the stack on top of yours [603.3b]. The choice of order for abilities controlled by the same player is made by that player [405.3].

results.question: I cast a sorcery with buyback and pay its buyback cost, then copy that spell with [Fork]. Once everything resolves, how many copies of the card end up back in my hand?
results.text: When you cast a sorcery with buyback and pay its buyback cost, the spell is put into your hand instead of your graveyard as it resolves [702.27a]. When Fork copies that spell, the copy is put onto the stack [707.10]. The copy of the spell is not cast [Fork ruling #9]. If you copy a spell for which buyback has been paid, you get nothing back because the copied spell does not have a card to give you [Fork ruling #8]. Therefore, only the original sorcery spell will end up back in your hand.

results.question: I have a face-down manifested card that's really [Lightning Bolt]. It dies and I imprint it on [Mimic Vat]. Later I activate Mimic Vat's copy ability -- do I get a token?
results.text: No, you will not get a token. Mimic Vat can only create a token that is a copy of a card exiled with it [Mimic Vat ruling #6]. If the exiled card is a nonpermanent card, no token is created [Mimic Vat ruling #0]. Since Lightning Bolt is an instant card, it is a nonpermanent card, and therefore Mimic Vat cannot create a token that is a copy of it.

results.question: My [Fiend Hunter]'s enters-the-battlefield ability is on the stack, about to exile a creature. I copy that ability with [Lithoform Engine] and target a second creature. Both get exiled. When Fiend Hunter later leaves the battlefield, do both come back?
results.text: Yes, both creatures will return to the battlefield. When Fiend Hunter's enters-the-battlefield ability is copied by Lithoform Engine, both the original ability and the copy exile a creature. These abilities are linked, meaning that when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield, its second ability will return all cards exiled by its first ability and its copies. Therefore, both creatures that were exiled will be returned to the battlefield under their owner's control.

results.question: My own [Banishing Light] has an opponent's creature exiled. On my opponent's turn I cast [Teferi's Protection], phasing out my Banishing Light. Does the exiled creature return to the battlefield?
results.text: When Teferi's Protection causes your permanents to phase out, any "until this leaves the battlefield" effects that are waiting to resolve will not happen. This means that if Banishing Light phases out before its triggered ability resolves, the exiled creature will not return to the battlefield. Phasing out does not cause "leaves the battlefield" abilities to trigger, and effects that are waiting for a permanent to leave the battlefield will not resolve when that permanent phases out. The exiled creature will return when Banishing Light phases back in, as the "until Banishing Light leaves the battlefield" effect will then end. Phased-out permanents phase back in before you untap during your untap step.

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. In response to its cast trigger, my opponent tries to [Counterspell] it. Can they even target it given protection from instants, and if it's countered, do I still control their next turn?
results.text: Your opponent can target Emrakul, the Promised End with Counterspell. Emrakul's "protection from instants" ability only applies while Emrakul is on the battlefield [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #2]. Since Emrakul is on the stack when your opponent casts Counterspell, it can be targeted. If Counterspell successfully resolves and counters Emrakul, Emrakul will be put into its owner's graveyard and will not resolve. Therefore, its triggered ability that causes you to gain control of an opponent will not happen, and you will not control their next turn [601.2i].

results.question: My cascade spell exiles cards until it hits [Valki, God of Lies], whose back face is the seven-mana planeswalker Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor. Is that a legal cascade hit, and can I cast the Tibalt side for free?
results.text: A cascade spell exiles cards until a nonland card with a mana value less than the cascade spell's mana value is exiled [702.85a]. When casting a double-faced spell, it is cast with its front face up by default [712.11c]. However, if an effect allows a player to cast a nonmodal double-faced card "transformed" or "converted," the resulting spell will have its back face up [712.8c]. The mana value of a double-faced spell is calculated using the mana cost of its front face [712.8c]. Therefore, even though Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor has a mana value of seven, Valki, God of Lies has a mana value of two. If your cascade spell has a mana value greater than two, and it exiles Valki, God of Lies, it is a legal cascade hit. However, you can only cast the Tibalt side for free if its mana value is less than the cascade spell's mana value [702.85a]. Since the mana value of Valki, God of Lies is used for this determination, you can only cast it for free if the cascade spell's mana value is greater than two.

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. With its cast trigger on the stack, I copy that trigger with [Lithoform Engine]. Then I untap Lithoform Engine with [Voltaic Key] and use it again to copy [Emrakul, the Promised End] itself as a permanent spell. How many of my opponent's turns do I control, do I get a second Emrakul, and does copying the Emrakul spell give me another control-a-turn trigger?
results.text: You will control one of your opponent's turns, and you will get a second Emrakul, the Promised End. Copying the Emrakul spell with Lithoform Engine does not give you another control-a-turn trigger because the trigger is part of the spell's casting, not the spell itself. When you cast Emrakul, the Promised End, its triggered ability goes on the stack [702.144a]. Lithoform Engine's ability targets an activated or triggered ability on the stack and creates another instance of that ability on the stack [Lithoform Engine ruling #3]. This means you will have two instances of Emrakul's "When you cast this spell" trigger on the stack. Lithoform Engine's ability to copy a permanent spell creates a copy of the spell on the stack [Lithoform Engine ruling #6]. This copy is then cast [707.12]. A copy of a permanent spell becomes a token as it resolves [111.13]. Therefore, you will have two Emrakul, the Promised End spells on the stack, one original and one copy that becomes a token. The original Emrakul's trigger will resolve, giving you control of an opponent's next turn and then that player an extra turn [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14]. The copy of Emrakul, the Promised End, when it resolves, will become a token and will not have a "When you cast this spell" trigger, as that trigger is associated with casting the spell, not with the spell resolving or a copy of the spell being created [707.10].

results.question: I've imprinted a creature on [Mimic Vat] and activate its ability to make a token copy. While that ability is on the stack, I copy it with [Lithoform Engine]. Do I get two tokens?
results.text: Yes, you will get two tokens. When you activate Mimic Vat's ability, you are creating a token that is a copy of a card exiled with Mimic Vat. This ability is put onto the stack [707.10]. Lithoform Engine's ability targets an activated ability on the stack and creates another instance of that ability on the stack [Lithoform Engine ruling #3]. This means you will have two separate abilities on the stack, each instructing you to create a token copy of a card exiled with Mimic Vat. When each of these abilities resolves, it will create a token that is a copy of a card exiled with Mimic Vat [707.10]. If no card has been exiled with Mimic Vat by the time an ability resolves, no token will be created [Mimic Vat ruling #6].

results.question: An opponent controls an untapped [Trinisphere], and I have a permanent that makes my green spells cost {1} less. I want to cast [Awaken the Woods] for value. If I cast it with X=0, what does it cost and what do I get, and what X should I actually choose?
results.text: To determine the total cost of casting Awaken the Woods with X=0, you first start with its mana cost, which is {X}{G}{G}. Since X=0, this is {0}{G}{G}. Then, you apply cost reductions. Your permanent makes green spells cost {1} less, so the {G} becomes {0}. The cost is now {0}{0}{0}. Finally, Trinisphere's effect is applied because the mana component of the spell's cost is less than three mana. Trinisphere increases the cost to three mana. Therefore, the total cost to cast Awaken the Woods with X=0 is {3}. You will get zero 1/1 green Forest Dryad land creature tokens because you cast it with X=0. To get any tokens, you should choose a value for X that is greater than 0. The rules do not specify what value of X you *should* choose, only how to calculate the cost for a chosen value of X.

results.question: [Grist, the Hunger Tide] is in my graveyard. Can I return it with [Animate Dead], and what happens?
results.text: Yes, you can return Grist, the Hunger Tide from your graveyard to the battlefield with Animate Dead. When Animate Dead enters the battlefield, it will cause Grist, the Hunger Tide to return to the battlefield under your control, and Animate Dead will attach to it. Grist, the Hunger Tide will enter the battlefield as a creature, as per its ability that states it is a creature in addition to its other types while not on the battlefield [Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1]. Animate Dead will then cause the enchanted creature to get -1/-0 [Animate Dead]. If Grist, the Hunger Tide would leave the battlefield, its controller sacrifices it due to Animate Dead's effect.

results.question: My commander [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] has four +1/+1 counters on it. It dies, I move it to the command zone, then recast it. Does it keep the counters, and does [Doubling Season] double them as it re-enters?
results.text: Skullbriar, the Walking Grave retains its counters when it moves to the command zone, as long as it is not moved to your hand or library first [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1]. When Skullbriar is recast and enters the battlefield, Doubling Season will double the number of counters it receives, as it affects permanents that enter with counters [Doubling Season ruling #2]. However, the counters Skullbriar already has on it do not get doubled by Doubling Season upon re-entering the battlefield; Doubling Season only affects counters that are put onto a permanent as it enters the battlefield [Doubling Season ruling #0].

results.question: I cast [Final Fortune] to take an extra turn. During that extra turn I use [Sundial of the Infinite] to end the turn before the end step. Do I still lose the game?
results.text: When you cast Final Fortune, you take an extra turn after the current one. At the beginning of that extra turn's end step, you lose the game [Final Fortune ruling #0]. However, if you use the Sundial of the Infinite's ability to end the turn before the end step, the end step is skipped [Sundial of the Infinite ruling #1]. Since the end step is skipped, the triggered ability that causes you to lose the game does not trigger, and you do not lose the game [Final Fortune ruling #1]. Ending the turn via the Sundial of the Infinite exiles all spells and abilities on the stack, removes creatures from combat, checks state-based actions, and then skips to the cleanup step [Sundial of the Infinite ruling #4]. Triggered abilities that would have triggered at the beginning of the end step will trigger at the beginning of the end step of the next turn instead [Sundial of the Infinite ruling #1].

results.question: I cast [Clone]. When and how do I choose what it copies, and can my opponent respond to that choice?
results.text: When you cast Clone, you choose what it copies as part of the process of it entering the battlefield. This choice is made when Clone is on the stack, but it doesn't become a copy until it enters the battlefield. Your opponent can respond to the spell being cast, but they cannot respond to the choice of what Clone will copy because that choice is made as it enters the battlefield, not as it is cast. Clone's ability does not target the creature it copies [Clone ruling #0]. If Clone enters the battlefield at the same time as another creature, you cannot choose that creature as the copy target, as you can only choose a creature already on the battlefield [Clone ruling #2]. You also have the option to not copy any creature, in which case Clone enters as a 0/0 creature and is likely put into the graveyard immediately [Clone ruling #5].

results.question: I activate my [Flooded Strand]'s ability, then activate [Gogo, Master of Mimicry] with X=2 to copy it twice. How many lands do I get from that one Flooded Strand?
results.text: When you activate Flooded Strand's ability, you search your library for a Plains or Island card, put it onto the battlefield, and then shuffle your library. Gogo, Master of Mimicry's ability copies an activated or triggered ability that is on the stack [Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #6]. In this case, Gogo copies the Flooded Strand's search ability twice. Each copy of the ability will instruct you to search your library for a Plains or Island card, put it onto the battlefield, and then shuffle your library [Flooded Strand]. Because the search instruction is being performed multiple times, rule [701.23h] states that this is the same as a single instruction to search that library for all those cards, and you search the library only once. However, the rule also states that any other instructions that refer to searching the zone still apply [701.23f]. Therefore, you will get one land from the initial activation, and then two additional lands from the two copies of the ability, for a total of three lands. Each of these searches will result in a shuffle of your library [Flooded Strand].
